questions.html: The principle of Locality of reference justifies the use of:
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Revision: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo

  • The principle of locality of reference states that programs tend to access the same set of memory locations repeatedly (temporal locality) or nearby memory locations (spatial locality).

  • Cache memory exploits this principle by keeping recently or frequently accessed instructions/data close to the CPU, reducing average memory access time.

 

So the justification of locality of reference is specifically for using cache memory.

questions.html: In a cache memory, if the total number of sets is ‘$s$’, then the set offset is:
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 2)

Cache memory we get #no of lines = size of cache / size of each block

next we find   # no of sets  if it is k way set assosiative

             # no of sets= no of lines/k=s

            set offset = No of bits require to index the set

                   set offset =log2(s).

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Detailed Video Solution: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo 

  • In cache memory, the set index (set offset) bits are determined by the number of sets.

  • If there are s sets, then we need $\log_2(s)$ bits to uniquely identify each set.

For example:

  • If s = 4, then set offset = $\log_2 4$ = 2 bits.

  • If s = 8, then set offset = $\log_2 8$ = 3 bits.

 So the correct option is $\log_2 s$.

Detailed Video Solution: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo

questions.html: A direct-mapped cache with $128$ KB of data is designed using $32$-bit addresses. The cache uses a block size of $4$ bytes. Each cache line has: A valid bit ($1$ bit), A tag field, data block. What is the total size of the cache (in bits), including both the data array and the tag array?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo

There are $2^{15}$ lines in cache, block size 32 bits, tag size $15$ bits. So, every cache line stores $32$ bits data, $15$ bits tag, $1$ valid bit.

Total cache size including both the data array and the tag array: $2^{15}$ * $48$ bits = $1.5$ Mbits.

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo

Source solution 2 (score: 4)

 

Tag directory size = (Number of cache blocks) × (Number of bits in the tag) + (Other bits per entry, i.e. Valid bits in this case)

                           = 2^15 * (15 + 1)

data array size = (Number of cache blocks) × (Number of bits in one block)

                         = 2^15 * (32 bits)   note: 4 byte = 4*8 bits given in question

hence total size of the cache (in bits), including both the data array and the tag array = 2^15(15+1 +32) = 1.5 Million bits

questions.html: Consider a machine with a byte-addressable main memory of $2^{16}$ bytes and a block size of $8$ bytes. Assume that a direct-mapped cache consisting of $32$ lines is used with this machine. How many bits will be there in Tag, line and word fields of the format of main memory addresses?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo

Given:

  • Main memory size = $2^{16}$ bytes

  • Block size = 8 bytes =$ 2^3$ → so word (block offset) = 3 bits

  • Cache lines = 32 = $2^5$ → so line (index) = 5 bits

Total address bits

Since memory size is $2^{16}$ bytes → we need 16 bits for the main memory address.

Word (block offset) bits

Block size = 8 bytes = $2^3$ → 3 bits.

Line (index) bits

Number of cache lines = 32 = $2^5$ → 5 bits.

Tag bits

Total = 16 bits.

So, Tag = 16 - (5+3) = 8 bits.

Final Answer = Tag = 8, Line = 5, Word = 3

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo

questions.html: Consider a small $2$-way set-associative cache memory, consisting of four blocks. For choosing the block to be replaced, use the least recently used (LRU) scheme. The number of cache misses for the following sequence of block addresses is $8, 12, 0, 12, 8$.
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/nUPpGN3nd5Y

$8$ - Compulsory/Cold Miss

$12$ - Compulsory/Cold Miss

$0$ - Compulsory/Cold Miss

$12$ - Hit

$8$ - Conflict Miss

We have $4$ blocks and $2$ blocks in a set

$\implies$ there are $2$ sets. So blocks will go to sets as follows:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf {Set Number} &  \textbf{Block Number} \\\hline \text{0} & \text{0,8,12}  \\\hline\text{1} &  \\\hline \end{array}$$
Since the lowest bit of block address is used for indexing into the set, so $8, 12$ and $0$ first miss in cache with $0$ replacing $8$ (there are two slots in each set due to $2-\text{way}$ set) and then $12$ hits in cache and $8$ again misses. So, totally $4$ misses.

Correct Answer: $C$

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/nUPpGN3nd5Y

questions.html: A cache memory needs an access time of $30$ ns and main memory $150$ ns, what is the average access time of the CPU (assume hit ratio $= 80\%$)?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo

Formula for average access time:

$$T_{avg} = (h \times T_c) + \big((1-h) \times (T_c + T_m)\big)$$
Where:

  • h = hit ratio = 0.8

  • $T_c$ = cache access time = $30\ \text{ns}$

  • $T_m$ = main memory access time = $150\ \text{ns}$

$$T_{avg} = (0.8 \times 30) + \big((0.2) \times (30 + 150)\big)$$

$$T_{avg} = 24 + (0.2 \times 180)$$

$$T_{avg} = 24 + 36 = 60 \ \text{ns}$$

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo

questions.html:
A two-way set associative cache memory unit with a capacity of $16\, KB$ is built using a block size of
$8\, words. $ The word length is $32-bits.$ The physical address space is $4\, GB.$
The number of bits in the TAG, SET fields are
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo

Given:

  • Cache capacity = $16 \, \text{KB} $

  • Word length = 32 bits = 4 bytes

  • Block size = $8 \, \text{words} = 8 \times 4 = 32 \, \text{bytes}$

  • Physical address space = $4 \, \text{GB} = 2^{32} \, \text{bytes}$

  • Cache type = 2-way set associative

Step 1: Number of blocks in cache

$$\text{Number of blocks} = \frac{\text{Cache size}}{\text{Block size}} = \frac{16384}{32} = 512 \, \text{blocks}$$

Step 2: Number of sets

Since it is 2-way set associative,

$$\text{Number of sets} = \frac{512}{2} = 256 = 2^8$$

So, Set field = 8 bits 

Step 3: Block offset (byte within block)

Block size = 32 bytes = 2^5 bytes → Block offset = 5 bits

Step 4: Address breakdown

Total physical address = 32 bits

$$\text{Tag bits} = 32 - (\text{Set bits} + \text{Block offset bits})$$

$$\text{Tag bits} = 32 - (8 + 5) = 19$$

So, Tag = 19 bits, Set = 8 bits 

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo

questions.html: A computer system uses $16-$bit memory addresses. It has a $16KB$ cache organised in a $4-$way set associative manner with $64 $ bytes per cache block. Assume that the size of each memory word is 2B. When a program is executed ,The processor reads data sequentially from the following byte addresses: $$128,144,2176,2180,128,2176$$ All the above addresses are shown in decimal values. Assume the cache is initially empty.  The number of addresses hit in the cache?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 5)

First, in these types of questions where a byte address is given, find the block number (the block to which the byte belongs). Then check which set that block maps to, and do the calculation:

  • Cache size = 16 KB = 16384 bytes.

  • Block size = 64 B → number of blocks in cache = 16384 / 64 = 256 blocks.

  • It's 4-way set associative → sets = 256 / 4 = 64 sets.

  • Block offset bits = 6 (64 B), index bits = 6 (64 sets), tag bits = 16−6−6 = 4.

Now map each byte address to a block (address ÷ 64) and check:

  1. 128 → block 2 (set 2) — miss (cold).

  2. 144 → block 2 (set 2) — hit (same block as 128).

  3. 2176 → block 34 (set 34) — miss (cold).

  4. 2180 → block 34 (set 34) — hit (same block as 2176).

  5. 128 → block 2 (set 2) — hit (block 2 still in cache).

  6. 2176 → block 34 (set 34) — hit (block 34 still in cache).

No set gets more than one distinct block in this sequence, so nothing gets evicted. That gives hits at accesses 2, 4, 5, 6 → 4 hits.

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

number of hits must be 2. The question should have been the number of misses for 4 to be answer.

once we find the address breakdown, we get format as:

To determine where a byte address maps inside the cache, we can find its memory block number and then extract its set index 

$$\text{Memory Block Number} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{Byte Address}}{64} \right\rfloor$$

$$\text{Set Index} = \text{Memory Block Number} \pmod{64}$$

questions.html:
Consider a computer with a $12$-bit address space and a byte-addressable memory. It has a data cache capable of holding eight cache blocks. Each cache block is $4$ bytes. During a particular program execution, the processor issues memory read instructions to the following sequence of block addresses:

$$
128,129,130,131,189,188,257,256,128,129,131,189,130, \text { and } 188 .
$$

If a $2$-way set-associative cache that uses the LRU-replacement algorithm and the cache is initially empty. The number of blocks that are hit in the cache of program is ____________
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 3)

2-way set-assoc → 8 blocks / 2 = 4 sets; set = block number mod 4:

Sets initially empty. Sequence (set index in parens):

  • 128(0) miss → set0: [128]

  • 129(1) miss → set1: [129]

  • 130(2) miss → set2: [130]

  • 131(3) miss → set3: [131]

  • 189(1) miss → set1: [129,189]

  • 188(0) miss → set0: [128,188]

  • 257(1) miss (evict LRU 129) → set1: [189,257]

  • 256(0) miss (evict LRU 128) → set0: [188,256]

  • 128(0) miss (evict LRU 188) → set0: [256,128]

  • 129(1) miss (evict LRU 189) → set1: [257,129]

  • 131(3) hit (131 still in set3)

  • 189(1) miss (evict LRU 257) → set1: [129,189]

  • 130(2) hit (130 still in set2)

  • 188(0) miss (188 was evicted earlier)

So only the accesses to 131 and 130 are hits → 2 hits.

questions.html: A $4$-way set-associative cache memory unit with a capacity of $16$ KB is built using a block size of $8$ words. The word length is $32$ bits. The size of the physical address space is $4$ GB. The number of bits for the TAG field is _________
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo 

Method 2 (Discussed in DVRUO Classes Cache Memory Lectures):

Number of sets$=\dfrac{\text{cache size}}{\text{size of a set}}$

Size of a set $=\text{block size}\times  \text{no. of blocks in a set}$

$= 8 \text{ words}\times 4\text{ (4-way set-associative)}$

$= 8\times 4\times 4\text{ (since a word is 32 bits = 4 bytes)}$

$= 128\text{ bytes}.$

So, number of sets $=\dfrac{16\ KB}{(128\ B)}=128$

Number of blocks in main memory = $4GB/32B = 2^{27}$

Now, we can divide the physical address space (i.e. main memory blocks) equally among these $128$ sets.

So, the number of main memory blocks that may possibly map to any particular set:

$=\dfrac{2^{27}}{128}$

$=2^{20}$

So, we need $20$ tag bits to identify one of these $2^{20}$ blocks.

Detailed Video Solution with Complete Analysis: https://youtu.be/jrt10F4jsWo
